items.summary:
ONE token turned a $0.40 AI request into $0.80.

and 4 "cheap" $20 subscriptions quietly cost $1,080 a year.

so i wrote 98 lines of python to audit what AI actually costs. real published prices, no vibes.

it said cut $360. the cache line alone was -88%.

here's what nobody checks.

ChatGPT Plus $20. Claude Pro $20. SuperGrok $30. Cursor Pro $20.
$90 a month. $1,080 a year. before tax.

each one looks reasonable the day you click subscribe. the bill only shows up when they stack

what the script printed, prices as of Aug 28, US web:

> 5M input + 1M output tokens a month: Sonnet 5 $20.00, Grok 4.6 $16.00, GPT-5.6 Luna $2.20
> use 1/5 of that and Sonnet is $4. not $20
> keep 2 subs + a $20 API budget: $720/yr. saves $360
> agent sending the same 100K prompt 50 times: $10.00 naive, $1.23 cached. -88%
> batch API: half price if you can wait
> Grok 4.6 at 199,999 tokens: $0.40. at 200,000: $0.80. one token doubles the whole request
> 20K records to JSON: $160 on Sol, $8.80 on Luna (my assumption: 1K in / 200 out each)

the lesson isn't "API is cheaper". heavy users burn $20 of API in days. the lesson is most people never did the math

how to audit yours:
1. list every AI sub and what you actually use it for
2. split the product (IDE, bots, connectors) from the model access
3. log 30 days of how often you open each one
4. move the occasional ones to pay-per-token
5. cache stable prompts, batch what can wait, watch the 200K / 272K cliffs
6. route easy work to cheap models, keep the frontier one for hard problems

every subscription has to earn its spot on your card. my math on published prices, not financial advice

🚨 A STRONG ECONOMY DOESN'T REQUIRE A STRONG STOCK MARKET AT EVERY PRICE

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
5) 🟠 BITCOIN - WE FINALLY HAVE MORE THAN 
A PRICE CHART TO EXAMINE

🟠 Bitcoin recovered above $80,000
🔍 We questioned whether the rebound had enough new buyers behind it

📅 November 6:
📉 BTC fell below $75,000 before recovering somewhat

🏦 US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $430 million in net outflows on November 5

📊 That was after a relatively small net inflow on November 4
⚠️ This doesn't prove that all investors are abandoning Bitcoin

🔄 ETF activity is only one part of the market

💸 But it does show that a major channel of investment demand was experiencing net withdrawals during the same period that the price recovery was losing strength

💡 That's much more useful than simply saying the chart looks bearish

🤔 Here's why:
⚖️ When sellers enter a market, the outcome depends partly on how much buying demand is waiting

🌊 In a deep market, substantial selling can be absorbed without an enormous price move
📉 In a thin market, selling can push prices down much faster

⚠️ If traders have also borrowed heavily to buy Bitcoin, falling prices may force them to close positions
💥 That creates additional selling

🔻 And if the market is still struggling to attract sustained spot demand, a temporary recovery can quickly reverse

🚨 THIS IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A PRICE REBOUND AND A CHANGE IN THE UNDERLYING BUYING TREND

🎯 Our August warning wasn't that Bitcoin could never rise
🔍 It was that sharp recoveries should not automatically be interpreted as proof that a fresh, durable wave of buyers has arrived

⚠️ The recent ETF withdrawals strengthen the case for caution

📊 But we still need to watch whether flows reverse, whether market depth improves and whether buying continues after leverage is reduced

🎯 THE NEXT IMPORTANT BITCOIN SIGNAL ISN'T ANOTHER GREEN CANDLE
💰 IT'S WHETHER REAL BUYERS CONTINUE SHOWING UP WHEN THE SELLERS RETURN

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
6) ✴️ MEXC - THE EXCHANGE IS OPERATING, BUT ITS ACCESS TO THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM IS UNDER THREAT

🇺🇸 On November 6, the US Treasury announced an order restricting financial transfers involving MEXC Global
⚖️ FinCEN alleges that the exchange facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions connected to sanctions evasion and other activities

👀 Now MEXC has responded
🛡️ The company says trading continues normally, customer assets remain secure and it intends to cooperate with regulators

🔍 Those statements don't necessarily contradict the US action

🚨 AN EXCHANGE CAN HOLD CUSTOMER ASSETS AND KEEP TRADING WHILE LOSING ACCESS TO IMPORTANT BANKING CHANNELS

🏦 The US order targets transfers involving American financial institutions

🌍 It does not automatically mean every customer account worldwide has been frozen

⚠️ Nor does MEXC's assurance that customer funds are safe remove the legal restrictions

📅 The order is scheduled to take effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register

🤔 Why should investors care?
🔗 Because crypto exchanges are businesses connected to both blockchains and the traditional financial system

💳 They need payment providers, banking partners, liquidity providers and counterparties willing to deal with them

💸 If those relationships weaken, a platform can face rising costs and reduced commercial flexibility even while its trading engine continues operating

⚖️ This is a business and regulatory risk 
- not proof of an immediate customer-asset loss

🔎 The next thing to watch is whether MEXC can preserve its operational relationships and respond effectively to the regulatory action

🎯 BLOCKCHAIN TRANSACTIONS CAN BE DECENTRALIZED
🏛️ THE BUSINESSES CONNECTING THEM TO THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM STILL FACE REAL-WORLD CONSTRAINTS

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🏁 THE REAL LESSON OF NOVEMBER 7

🌍 This week brought several very different developments
- 🇮🇷 Iran intensified diplomacy
- 🏦 AI lenders began testing the market for existing debt
- 🇺🇸 The US labor market proved stronger than expected
- 🟠 Bitcoin's recovery faced renewed selling
- ⚖️ And a major crypto exchange faced restrictions on access to US finance

🔍 These events aren't all caused by the same thing
💡 But they reveal an important distinction between what markets expect and what economies can actually deliver

🛢️ A peace agreement can change oil futures immediately
🏗️Damaged energy facilities still need years of repair

🇺🇦 A diplomatic announcement can change expectations
🛡️Security guarantees still need financing and enforcement

🤖 An AI company can raise billions
💵Its infrastructure still needs customers and sufficient revenue to repay its costs

🇺🇸 A strong economy can lift corporate earnings
💵Expensive financing can still pressure stock valuations

🟠 Bitcoin can rally
⚠️A sustainable advance still requires sufficient buying demand

✴️ A crypto exchange can keep operating
🏦Its access to banking infrastructure can still deteriorate

🚨 THE MARKET PRICES WHAT IT EXPECTS TO HAPPEN
💰 CAPITAL EVENTUALLY HAS TO PAY FOR WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS

🎯 And that's the gap we're watching
🔎 Not just who promises the next great opportunity

⚖️ But who is building something necessary, who is paying for it, who is receiving the revenue 
- and who is left carrying the risk

🙉 SURVIVE FIRST

items.title: Jensen Huang says engineers should burn $250,000 of AI a year, and Apple just cut its engineers' AI budget to about $50,
items.summary:
Jensen Huang says engineers should burn $250,000 of AI a year, and Apple just cut its engineers' AI budget to about $50,000.

And Apple plans to cut it again.

Last month, some Apple engineers saw their daily AI spending cap drop from $300 to $200, Bloomberg reported. Some engineering teams could be cut to $100 a day next. Many groups outside engineering already sit at $100, and Apple has considered going as low as $25 for some of them.

In March, Jensen said on the All-In podcast that he'd be deeply alarmed if a $500,000 engineer used less than $250,000 of AI tokens in a year. He also said Dario Amodei's forecast of hundreds of billions in AI revenue was too conservative.

So Jensen's rule is simple: AI spending should run about half of what an engineer gets paid.

By my math, at about 250 workdays a year, $200 a day comes to roughly $50,000. The planned $100 cap comes to roughly $25,000.

By Jensen's rule, a $100 daily cap only makes sense for an engineer paid about $50,000 a year.

And Apple still wants its people using MORE AI. It's steering teams toward cheaper models and AI that runs on the device, and Bloomberg's Mark Gurman has said Apple's internal work runs heavily on Anthropic's models.

I think Apple just showed where the real limit on the AI boom sits now: The finance department.

And that's just ONE company:

- Accenture capped Claude at $29 a month per employee on October 1, after some staff had been spending up to $1,000 a month, 404 Media reported.
- Uber burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in about 4 months, then capped AI coding tools at $1,500 a month per tool.
- Microsoft has cut allowances too, and its AI chief Mustafa Suleyman told Bloomberg that Anthropic is extremely expensive and that Microsoft wants to eventually get rid of that cost.
- Meta had internal leaderboards ranking staff by how many tokens they used, and now it has introduced token budgets.

The usage is clearly there. Uber's engineers used the tools so much they spent a full year's budget in 4 months.

So the people saying stop are the ones paying the bill.

That's a huge problem for the AI labs, for one reason: Their spending is already locked in. 

Anthropic has committed to $895 billion, mostly for computing power. OpenAI has signed more than $1.4 trillion of compute deals. And paying for all of it depends on companies spending more on AI per worker every year.

Apple, Accenture, Uber and Microsoft all pay for Anthropic's models, and Anthropic could start its IPO roadshow as early as next week. Its own filing shows revenue grew about 47% from the second quarter to the third, down from about 144% the quarter before, and price cuts took about $600 million out of revenue.

Plenty of people will say this is just housekeeping, and they have numbers:

Bloomberg says few Apple engineers ever used the full $300, so the savings may be small. Cheaper models can do the same work for less. Apple's R&D still rose 32% to $45.8 billion in fiscal 2026, partly because of AI. And more companies start using AI every month, so total spending can keep growing even with a cap on each worker.

But Jensen's pitch depends on spending per worker going UP. Apple, Microsoft, Meta, Uber and Accenture are all writing rules that push it down.

So the first question for Anthropic's roadshow should be simple: How much are its biggest customers spending per employee compared with a year ago, and how many of them have put caps in place?

Who's right about what an engineer's AI is worth, Jensen Huang or Apple's finance team?
